https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.text: Figure caption, Watch: Modi tells Putin "move on from an endless war to an end of war" Published 4 hours ago Russian President Vladimir Putin has been urged by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a close ally, to end Moscow's war against Ukraine. "Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said on Monday. Modi, whose country's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow, has made several similar pleas to Putin since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. BBC correspondents in Delhi and Moscow look at what lies behind Modi's renewed appeal for peace, and Putin's response. By Vikas Pandey India digital editor, Delhi Modi's comments on ending the war in Ukraine are not surprising and don't suggest any tactical change in India's foreign policy. In fact, speaking on the sidelines of a regional summit in 2022 - less than a year into the conflict - Modi told Putin publicly that "now is not the time for war". But it would be an oversimplification to suggest that Modi's current or past statements on the war can be seen as a rebuff to Putin or Russia's strategy. Western countries have pushed Modi hard to take a clear stand on the war - but Delhi has largely stayed neutral, urging dialogue to end the war instead. The stand hasn't made many Western capitals happy but they have continued to court Modi and India - it's just too big and too fast-growing an economy to be ignored. In this context, Modi's current statement cannot be seen as an attempt to please a third country. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, India's economy relies heavily on imported Russian oil If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly? The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses. Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades. Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries. But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association. Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs. So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats. As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war. By Steve Rosenberg Russia editor, Moscow This isn't the first time a foreign leader has publicly urged Putin to end the war in Ukraine. Just five weeks ago the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev suggested Putin freeze the conflict and return to the negotiating table. He didn't. And he hasn't. There's no sign of these public calls for peace changing Putin's calculations. To Modi's call for a cessation of hostilities, the Kremlin leader replied: "Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path." Polite, but vague. And non-committal. After all, a path can be short. But it can also be long. Very long. And "moving forward" at what pace? And, crucially, on which path? All the evidence suggests that Russia's leadership remains convinced it is on a path to military victory in Ukraine. To frame that in terms of peace, "moving forward" to peace on Russia's terms dictated by military success. Therefore, for now, the fighting goes on. Despite the fact that, after more than four-and-a-half years of war and huge military losses, the Kremlin has yet to secure victory. And despite Ukraine's success in bringing the war back home to Russians: for example, through long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries that have sparked fuel shortages and petrol queues across the country. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Four people were killed in overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine's town of Boryspil, outside Kyiv In recent days Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine. "After [Russia] intensified its strikes on Ukraine's military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure," wrote the Kommersant newspaper this morning, "the Russian side is convinced that in the military confrontation time is working against Kyiv." While Putin believes that, he'll be reluctant to pause his so-called "special military operation". https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv0l.text: Image source, AFP Image caption, Yemen's government said the missile strike killed recruits to its internal security forces (file photo) By David Gritten Published 5 hours ago More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say. A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police. The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response". The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations". Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months. At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis. With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September. However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces. The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia. Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says Published 3 days ago On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged Published 7 days ago 'We are terrified but we want to get an education', say Yemeni schoolgirls Published 6 October Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation. Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added. A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground. Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target. He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes". The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities. In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children. According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks. The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August. In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. https://londonlovesbusiness.com/kremlin-.text: Tech Property Business London Loves Darek Delmanowicz/PAP/Avalon Business News Defence Politics News World News Kremlin-linked network accused of amplifying tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv by Elsa Mcintosh, Defence and Security Editor October 10, 2026 written by Elsa Mcintosh, Defence and Security Editor 10 th Oct 26 1:37 pm Russia has intensified its information campaign against Ukraine ahead of Poland’s Independence Day, seeking to exploit strains between Warsaw and Kyiv and cultivate the impression that Polish public support for its eastern neighbour is beginning to fracture, according to Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation. The Ukrainian agency said the Russian-linked disinformation network Pravda, also known as Portal Kombat, was circulating narratives portraying Polish-Ukrainian relations as having deteriorated sharply. The messages promote claims of a collapse in bilateral friendship, rising xenophobia towards Ukrainians in Poland and growing public fatigue with support for Kyiv. According to the agency, the campaign seeks to turn disagreements between the neighbouring countries into evidence of a much broader political rupture — one that could weaken international backing for Ukraine as its war with Russia continues. The allegations highlight a central feature of Moscow’s confrontation with Kyiv: the battle for European support is being fought not only through military operations and diplomatic pressure, but also through attempts to shape how European societies perceive the costs and consequences of the war. Read more related news: Royal Navy chief delivers damning warning to Burnham over Britain’s defences Burnham told to ‘wake up’ and warned Putin is plotting ‘something bad’ A nuclear power with a water pistol as Royal Navy’s reported drone defence sparks alarm Bodies on the road, profits on the table: Ukraine’s horror exposes the moral cost of negotiating with Putin The Center for Countering Disinformation said the campaign was part of a systematic Russian effort to amplify divisions between partner countries and create an exaggerated impression of hostility. By presenting disputes as evidence that solidarity with Ukraine is collapsing, the Kremlin seeks to undermine confidence in the durability of European support, the agency argued. Poland’s Independence Day provides a politically sensitive moment for such messaging. Questions of national identity, historical memory and relations with neighbouring states carry particular significance in Poland, where support for Ukraine has coexisted with disagreements over history and the practical consequences of the war. The alleged operation also draws on tensions that have become more visible in diplomatic relations between Warsaw and Kyiv. Piotr Łukasiewicz, Poland’s chargé d’affaires in Ukraine, said relations between the two countries had moved in 2026 from one of their strongest periods to one of their weakest. He attributed part of the deterioration to disputes over shared history, particularly the activities of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army and the legacy of Stepan Bandera, a prominent figure in the Ukrainian nationalist movement of the 20th century. These historical disputes are politically consequential because the two countries interpret parts of their shared past differently. Episodes associated with Ukrainian nationalist movements remain deeply contentious in Poland, while their place in Ukraine’s national historical narrative is shaped by a different experience of national struggle and Soviet domination. Such disagreements can complicate an otherwise strategically important partnership . Poland has been a key neighbour and supporter of Ukraine, while Kyiv’s pursuit of European Union membership gives the relationship an additional institutional dimension. Łukasiewicz nevertheless stressed that historical debates were not currently part of negotiations over Ukraine’s accession to the EU. That distinction matters. Diplomatic friction over historical memory does not, by itself, establish that Poland is abandoning support for Ukraine or that the two governments’ broader strategic interests have fundamentally diverged. Nor do the claims identified by the Ukrainian agency establish that Polish society has turned decisively against Kyiv. The allegations concern messages being circulated within Poland’s information environment, rather than independently verified evidence of a wholesale collapse in public support . The strategic risk , according to the Ukrainian assessment, lies in the gap between genuine disagreements and the sweeping conclusions that disinformation networks seek to draw from them. A dispute over historical responsibility can be presented as proof that a partnership has failed. Criticism of government policy can be recast as widespread hostility towards Ukrainians. Individual disagreements can be amplified until they appear to represent an irreversible national shift. The objective is not necessarily to invent every grievance, but to magnify existing divisions, strip them of context and make cooperation appear increasingly untenable. For Moscow, that approach offers a potential means of weakening Ukraine’s international position without achieving a comparable result on the battlefield. If European governments and public’s become less willing to sustain political , financial or military support for Kyiv, Russia could gain strategic room for manoeuvre. The challenge for Warsaw and Kyiv is therefore twofold: manage their genuine disputes without allowing them to overwhelm areas of common interest, while ensuring that claims circulating online are assessed against verifiable evidence rather than repetition. The Ukrainian agency’s warning does not prove that Russia has succeeded in changing Polish public opinion. It does, however, underline the importance Moscow appears to attach to the political cohesion of Ukraine’s European partners. The broader contest is over whether disagreements between allies remain manageable differences — or are transformed into evidence that the alliance itself is coming apart.
